lede: Oil takes back Friday's deal rally; gold drops 3% on rates.
geo_headlines: OIL IS TAKING BACK FRIDAY'S DEAL RALLY - AND THEN SOME. Brent is $108.46 (+4.0%) and WTI $96.29 (+4.2%) this morning, more than reversing Friday's 2% drop, after Trump rejected Iran's Hormuz plan and Tehran said it will not soften its conditions. **Brent is up almost 18% this month** (Reuters). Diesel is at record highs in the US and Europe on refining shortages - the channel into embedded inflation the Fed worries about.

BOTH SIDES TALKED TOUGH AND LEFT A DOOR OPEN. Araghchi on Meet the Press: "We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed... At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose." He floated Iran's 60% enriched uranium as a possible future bargaining chip. Trump said new strikes before the midterms are "possible" but told Axios he expects talks to resume this week; Qatar is mediating and the Saudi foreign minister has arrived in Washington (Iran International).

THE BARRELS ARE MOVING FASTER THAN THE DIPLOMACY. Kpler data via Reuters: Middle East crude exports rebounded to 12.8 million barrels a day in September, the most since the war began, with Hormuz flows about 7.4 million and Saudi exports more than doubling to 5.4 million. Regional exports are still about 6 million barrels a day below February. Bessent on Fox: once Iran makes its final deliveries to China, "they will have nothing."

GOLD IS DOWN 3% - THE CLEAREST SIGN THIS IS A RATES STORY, NOT A FEAR STORY. Gold futures $4,188.50 (-3.1%); Reuters had spot at $4,171.85, down 2.7%, on bets the Fed keeps hiking. The dollar index is at a two-month high of 101.39. Higher oil means higher inflation expectations, which means higher real yields - and gold, which pays nothing, loses. Bitcoin is down 1.8% to $82,970.

BONDS ARE STILL UNDER PRESSURE BEFORE THE WEEK'S DATA. Reuters: the 30-year Treasury touched 5.5173% overnight, near its highest since 2004 and up 27bp this month; the 2-year is up 55bp this month. FedWatch still shows Friday's 64.2% October hike odds; Reuters cites a 68% market-implied chance. Bank of America's Cabana: repricing may not stop until financial conditions are "sufficiently restrictive." Atlanta Fed GDPNow: 5.0%.

FUTURES SLIP, ASIA MIXED, EUROPE SHRUGS. S&P futures -0.48%, Nasdaq futures -0.85%. Korea's Kospi -2.7% and Shanghai -1.7% led Asia lower, with Chinese tech hit by a US bill barring Chinese AI data-centre components from sensitive government systems; China's August industrial profit growth slowed to 4.2%, its weakest of the year. Nikkei -0.7%. Europe opened higher, led by UK homebuilders on a new buyer-support scheme.

TODAY IS QUIET ON DATA: TWO FED SPEAKERS AND JEFFERIES. Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman speaks on bank supervision at 8:15 AM and Governor Cook on AI at 1:25 PM. Jefferies reports third-quarter results after the close (company IR), the first read on investment-banking fees this season. The heavy data starts Tuesday with JOLTS; the week ends with Friday's payrolls, expected around 85,000 with unemployment at 4.1%.
client_frame_short: The weekend headlines are now showing up in prices. Oil is up about 4% this morning because the Iran deal that markets hoped for on Friday was publicly rejected, and gold is down 3% because higher oil means higher interest rates for longer. **Stock futures are down only about half a percent, which tells you the market sees this as an inflation and rates story, not a crisis.** Both sides are still talking about talks this week. Nothing here calls for action; Wednesday's inflation report and Friday's jobs report will matter more than today's oil price.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, start with what they will see on the screen: oil sharply higher, gold sharply lower, stocks slightly lower. Those three moves tell one coherent story.

Oil first. On Friday Brent fell about 2% on hopes that Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz would be accepted. Over the weekend the President rejected it, and Iran said it would not soften its terms. So this morning Brent is back at about $108, up 4%, and it has risen almost 18% this month. Diesel is at record highs because refining is short. That is what reaches household budgets and, eventually, the Fed.

The part clients rarely hear is that physical oil is flowing better than the headlines suggest. Industry tracking data show Middle East crude exports this month at their highest since the war began, with Saudi shipments more than doubling from August. Supply is still well below where it was in February, but the trend is improving, and both governments say talks could resume this week.

Gold is the tell. If investors were frightened, gold would be rising. Instead it is down 3%, because higher oil means higher inflation, higher inflation means the Fed keeps raising rates, and higher rates make an asset that pays no interest less attractive. The 30-year Treasury yield is near its highest since 2004. The market is pricing more tightening, not a panic.

Stocks are absorbing it calmly: S&P futures are down about half a percent after last week's 1.2% gain, and the S&P 500 is 0.71% below its August 13 record. The advice stays steady. Yields above 5% are a real opportunity for idle cash, and portfolios built for an inflationary, higher-rate world do not need changing because of one weekend. What would change the view: Brent holding above $110, a 10-year close above 5.25%, or a hot August PCE report on Wednesday.
